metadata.title: SynonymLens — Curated Vocabulary Starter Dataset
metadata.description: A teacher-curated starter set ordered from very common to less common academic vocabulary. Every listed sense has its own definition, original example, sense-matched synonyms, and antonyms or clearly labeled contrasts.
metadata.scope_note: This is a curated starter set, not an exhaustive dictionary. Frequency bands are pedagogical relative bands, not measured corpus ranks. Synonyms are sense-specific and include fit/register notes; antonyms are supplied only where a useful opposite or contrast exists.

field_guide.frequency_band: Relative learning order: very_common, common, less_common.
field_guide.cefr: Approximate learner level for the listed sense.
field_guide.definitions: Each object is one part-of-speech-specific sense. Add a separate object for each additional sense so examples and relations stay attached to the correct meaning.
field_guide.synonyms.fit: Explains the context in which the synonym can replace the headword.
field_guide.antonyms.relationship: direct = clear lexical opposite; contrast = useful opposing idea, but not a strict antonym.

metadata.source_note: Definitions and example sentences in this starter set are original concise editorial content. Relative frequency bands are teacher-curated and should be replaced with a corpus frequency value if the site needs objective ranking.

definitions.definition: of a high standard or producing a positive result
definitions.example: The new reading program has had a *good* effect on students' confidence.

synonyms.fit: Works for effects, results, or changes; more formal than good.
Emphasizes that something helps or improves a situation; more formal.

antonyms.fit: General opposite for quality or effect.
Use when the effect causes damage rather than benefit.

definitions.definition: unpleasant, harmful, or of a low standard
definitions.example: A lack of sleep can have a *bad* effect on concentration.

synonyms.fit: Fits effects, results, or consequences; more neutral and formal.
Use when something causes damage to health, people, or the environment.

antonyms.fit: General opposite for quality or effect.
Use when something produces a helpful effect.

definitions.definition: having a strong effect, great value, or a necessary role
definitions.example: Regular feedback plays an *important* role in language learning.

synonyms.fit: Use for a noticeable effect, amount, or meaning; not usually in 'It is significant to...'.
Use when something is essential for success or an outcome; stronger than important.

antonyms.fit: Plain opposite meaning: having little value or effect.
Use before a noun for something of lesser importance or scale.

definitions.definition: large in size, amount, or degree
definitions.example: The city faces a *big* challenge in reducing traffic congestion.

synonyms.fit: Neutral replacement for physical size or amount; less conversational than big.
Use for a large amount, change, or effect; formal and often measurable.

antonyms.fit: Opposite for size, amount, or degree.
Use for a problem, change, or role that is limited in scale.

definitions.definition: limited in size, amount, or degree
definitions.example: Even a *small* change in daily habits can improve health over time.

synonyms.fit: Use for a limited problem, difference, or change; not usually for physical size.
Emphasizes that the amount, range, or effect is restricted.

antonyms.fit: General opposite for size or degree.
Use for an amount or effect that is large and meaningful.

definitions.definition: to make or become different
definitions.example: The school plans to *change* its assessment system next year.

synonyms.fit: Use for making a specific adjustment; slightly more formal.
Use when making a partial or controlled change to a plan, rule, or design.

antonyms.fit: Use when something remains as it is.
Use when deliberately protecting something from change.

definitions.definition: to make it easier for someone to do something or for something to happen
definitions.example: Visual examples can *help* learners understand abstract ideas.

synonyms.fit: A more formal alternative, especially when a person provides support.
Use when providing ongoing help, encouragement, or resources.

antonyms.fit: To make progress or an action more difficult.
To block progress or prevent an action.

definitions.definition: a situation or matter that is difficult and needs attention or a solution
definitions.example: Rising housing costs have become a serious *problem* for young families.

synonyms.fit: A neutral, often more diplomatic term for a matter needing attention.
Use when emphasizing difficulty that requires effort, not necessarily a defect.

antonyms.fit: The answer or method that resolves a problem.
An opposing idea in evaluation: a benefit rather than a difficulty.

definitions.definition: to make something happen, especially something unwanted
definitions.example: Heavy traffic can *cause* delays for emergency services.

synonyms.fit: Natural alternative for describing a result or consequence.
Formal alternative followed by an outcome or noun phrase.

antonyms.fit: To stop something from happening.
To prevent a harmful event, often through timely action.

definitions.definition: to make information or a fact clear or visible
definitions.example: The survey results *show* that many students prefer flexible study hours.

synonyms.fit: Use when evidence or an example makes a point clear; formal.
Use when evidence points toward a conclusion without proving it completely.

antonyms.fit: To keep something from being seen or known.
A more formal alternative to hide.

definitions.definition: to become better or make something better
definitions.example: The city is investing in public transport to *improve* air quality.

synonyms.fit: Use when making quality, value, or effectiveness better; formal.
Use for skills, systems, relationships, or evidence that become stronger.

antonyms.fit: To become or make something worse.
To gradually become worse in quality or condition; formal.

definitions.definition: a change or result produced by an action or event
definitions.example: Researchers are studying the *effects* of screen time on children's sleep.

synonyms.fit: Use when emphasizing a strong or important effect.
Use for a result that follows an action, often an important or indirect one.

antonyms.fit: The reason something happens, rather than the result.
The starting point of something, rather than its resulting effect.

definitions.definition: to make something smaller in amount, size, number, or intensity
definitions.example: Car-sharing schemes may *reduce* the number of vehicles on the road.

synonyms.fit: A close alternative for amounts, numbers, or levels.
Common with prices, rates, levels, and standards.

antonyms.fit: To make an amount, number, or level greater.
Common with prices, rates, levels, and standards.

definitions.definition: an advantage or helpful effect that something provides
definitions.example: One major *benefit* of learning online is the flexibility it offers.

synonyms.fit: A general positive feature compared with another option.
Use for a valuable quality, resource, or feature; often formal.

antonyms.fit: A feature that makes something less useful or desirable.
A specific negative feature or limitation.

definitions.definition: to grow, progress, or make something more advanced over time
definitions.example: Schools can help students *develop* critical-thinking skills.

synonyms.fit: Natural for skills, confidence, relationships, and capacity.
Use for deliberately helping a quality, habit, or skill grow; formal.

antonyms.fit: To weaken the growth, success, or effectiveness of something.
To become weaker or less successful over time.

definitions.definition: large or important enough to have a noticeable effect or meaning
definitions.example: The policy led to a *significant* reduction in workplace injuries.

synonyms.fit: Use for a large amount, degree, or change; often measurable.
Use for an amount or degree that is fairly large.

antonyms.fit: Too small or unimportant to have a noticeable effect.
So small that it can be ignored; stronger than insignificant for amounts.

definitions.definition: large in amount, value, or importance
definitions.example: The project requires a *substantial* investment of time and money.

synonyms.fit: A close formal alternative for a fairly large amount or degree.
Use when the amount is large enough to matter or produce an effect.

antonyms.fit: General opposite for amount or size.
Use when an amount is so small it has little practical effect.

definitions.definition: producing a helpful or positive effect
definitions.example: Regular physical activity is *beneficial* to both physical and mental health.

synonyms.fit: Use when something gives a person or group an advantage.
A simpler, more conversational alternative.

antonyms.fit: Producing damage or a negative effect.
A formal alternative meaning harmful to something.

definitions.definition: causing harm or damage to something
definitions.example: Long-term exposure to noise can be *detrimental* to children's learning.

synonyms.fit: The clearest everyday alternative.
Emphasizes a harmful effect that may be serious or lasting.

antonyms.fit: Producing a helpful or positive effect.
Producing a benefit or giving an advantage.

definitions.definition: to make an action or process easier to do or achieve
definitions.example: Clear public information can *facilitate* access to health services.

synonyms.fit: Use when something makes an action possible, not merely easier.
A shorter alternative meaning to make something less difficult.

antonyms.fit: To make an action or process more difficult.
To make something more difficult by adding problems or steps.

definitions.definition: to make a harmful effect, problem, or risk less severe
definitions.example: Planting trees can help *mitigate* the effects of extreme heat in cities.

synonyms.fit: A clear general alternative meaning to reduce in degree.
Common with pain, hardship, pressure, or suffering.

antonyms.fit: To make a problem or condition more severe.
A formal alternative meaning to make a problem worse.

definitions.definition: to make a bad situation, problem, or illness more severe
definitions.example: A shortage of affordable housing may *exacerbate* inequality.

synonyms.fit: The simplest and most widely understood alternative.
Use for a problem, conflict, or condition made more serious.

antonyms.fit: To make a situation better rather than worse.
To make a problem or suffering less severe.

definitions.definition: to make pain, hardship, or a problem less severe
definitions.example: Targeted financial support can *alleviate* the pressure on low-income households.

synonyms.fit: A common alternative for reducing pain, pressure, or difficulty.
Common with pain, stress, symptoms, and pressure.

antonyms.fit: To make a feeling, problem, or effect stronger.
To make a problem more severe; formal.

definitions.definition: common or widespread in a particular place, group, or period
definitions.example: Remote work is increasingly *prevalent* in technology companies.

synonyms.fit: A close, accessible alternative for something found in many places or among many people.
A simpler alternative; less formal and less emphatic.

antonyms.fit: Not happening or existing often.
Not frequently found or experienced.

definitions.definition: available only in small amounts or numbers
definitions.example: Clean water becomes *scarce* during prolonged droughts.

synonyms.fit: A neutral alternative emphasizing a restricted supply or amount.
A common phrase for something that is not available in sufficient amounts.

antonyms.fit: Available in large quantities.
Existing in large amounts or numbers.

definitions.definition: able to continue over time without exhausting resources or causing serious harm
definitions.example: Cities need *sustainable* transport systems that reduce pollution and remain affordable.

synonyms.fit: Use when a plan or system can work successfully over time; does not always include environmental meaning.
Use specifically for resources that can be naturally replaced, such as wind or solar energy.

antonyms.fit: Unable to continue over time without serious cost or damage.
Use for a practice that uses up resources faster than they can be replaced.
